summary: We are testing whether a composite optimization (unified time allocation removing the 60/40 phase split, position-level early termination, fast I/O, and random-restart ordering diversity) improves polyomino packing scores over the well-established v7 baseline. The v7 baseline has been measured at ~83 across three prior iterations, and the prediction is a marginal +1-3 point improvement from v10.
key_points: Two arms: h-main (v10 with unified sweep + early termination + fast I/O + random restart) vs h-control-negative (v7 baseline, expected score 79-86, mean ~83).

The core mechanism: v7 reserves 40% of its 2s time budget for alternative orderings at fixed widths; v10 eliminates this reservation, giving the primary width sweep ~66% more time, while early termination makes each pack() call ~10-20% faster, enabling exploration of 1-3 additional widths.

Confirmation: v10 scores measurably higher than v7 in a paired comparison (predicted +1-3 points average). Refutation: v10 scores equal or lower, suggesting the 60/40 phase split's ordering diversity was more valuable than extra width-sweep coverage.

Known risk: the ~6-point noise floor (from system load variance, observed in iter-3) may mask a small improvement. Single-seed measurements per arm limit statistical power, but this is a cost-conscious tier-2 experiment.

Diagnostic plan if v10 underperforms: check whether the removed alt-ordering phase was critical for medium instances (n=300-1000), whether random restart adds overhead on small instances, or whether early termination has a correctness bug skipping valid positions.
